notes: West leads the ♣10 against 3NT. At first glance an overtrick appears likely with 5 hearts tricks (assuming at worst a 4-2 break), 3 diamond tricks, and 2 club tricks. The blockage in the heart suit and the lack of entries to the closed hand will result in the defeat of the contract, however, if South is not careful.

It seems natural for South to play a low club from the dummy at trick 1. When East follows low South wins the trick and leads a heart to dummy's ♥A. The ♥J comes next, but neither of South's options on this trick will lead to success given the 4-2 heart break.

If the ♥J is allowed to win the trick, South will have no way to return to his hand to enjoy his other 3 heart winners. If instead South overtakes the ♥J with the ♥K or ♥Q, West will discard on the third round of hearts and East's control of the fourth round of that suit will leave South with no hope for the contract.

South can, in fact, guarantee his contract by winning the first trick with dummy's ♣A. South should continue by winning the next 2 tricks with dummy's ♥A and ♥J, unblocking the suit. South has retained both the ♣Q and ♣J in the closed hand and he can now force an entry to his long hearts by leading a club; it makes no difference whether the defenders win their ♣K or hold up.

West returns a club which South wins in hand. South is now able to cash 3 more heart winners followed by 3 diamond tricks to emerge with an overtrick. The defense could have prevented the overtrick by cashing 3 rounds of spades after winning the ♣K, but the contract was never in danger once South made the unusual (delayed) entry-preserving play of rising with the ♣A at trick 1.

notes: West leads the ♠J against 1NT. There are 5 top tricks (2 spades, 2 hearts, and the ♦A). South's long clubs will provide more than enough tricks for the contract once the ♣A and ♣K are dislodged. South must make the correct play at trick 1, however, or the contract will be in danger.

If South makes the natural "second hand low" play and wins the ♠K in the closed hand and then starts on clubs, the defense will duck the first round of that suit. West will win the second round of clubs and continue spades to drive out dummy's ♠A. South will have only 1 entry back to his hand (the ♥K) which will not be enough to establish the clubs and then later enjoy them.

South can always make 1NT, but he must win West's spade opening lead with dummy's ♠A in order to preserve the ♠K as an entry to the closed hand. South should start clubs by leading dummy's ♣Q and now it will not help the defense to duck this trick (or to win it for that matter). West wins the second round of clubs and plays a second spade to South's ♠K.

With the lead conveniently placed in the South hand, clubs can be established by knocking out the remaining honor. West is welcome to cash his 3 spade winners, but South will later by able to get to his hand with the ♥K in order to enjoy 3 more club tricks. South will actually end up with an overtrick as a result of his careful play to the first trick.

notes: West leads the ♠J against 3NT. There are 6 top tricks (3 spades and 3 hearts). The diamond suit has the potential to deliver 5 extra tricks after the ♦A is dislodged. After winning West's spade opening lead in dummy, the natural continuation is to play a low diamond to South's ♦K.

If West, who must have the ♦A given his opening bid, wins the trick there will be no further problems if the East-West diamonds were originally distributed 3-2. If West was dealt a singleton ♦A, however, the contract will fail. On this layout East will have to win a second diamond trick for the defense before South can establish the suit. The defense will then be able to take 3 club tricks to defeat the contract.

Careful play is required to guard against this diamond layout. South should cross to his hand in hearts at trick 2 and start the diamonds by leading the ♦2 toward the dummy. If West has the singleton ♦A he will win the trick and play another spade to the dummy. South can continue by unblocking the ♦K, cashing the ♠Q, and using dummy's ♥A as an entry to dummy's remaining diamond winners.

If West was dealt 2 or 3 diamonds headed by the ♦A, he will duck the first round of the suit and dummy's ♦Q or ♦J will win the trick. South can continue with a diamond to his ♦K and West will duck again if he is able to. South is now able to cross to the dummy and lead a third round of diamonds to establish the suit. The dummy's remaining entry can be used to access the rest of the diamonds.

notes: West leads the ♥Q against 4♠. West would not lead the ♥Q if he held the ♥A as well, so it would be a mistake for South to cover with dummy's ♥K at trick 1. East would win the ♥A and the defense would win the next 2 tricks in hearts. South would then have to lose at least 1 trump trick and the contract would fail.

South should play a low heart from both hands at trick 1. South's ♥10 makes it unsafe for West to continue hearts, so West will switch to a club which South wins with the ♣A. Dummy's diamond suit will eventually provide a parking place for at least 1 of South's heart losers, so South must focus his attention on playing the trump suit for only 1 loser. Both defenders follow small when South cashes the ♠A.

If both defenders have 2 spades left there is no way for South to avoid losing 2 trump tricks. Similarly, if either defender has 3 or more spades left headed by the ♠K and ♠J, 2 trump tricks will also have to be lost. If the ♠K is now singleonton the best South can do is to continue with a small spade from his hand. This will not be good enough, however, as the defense will take the ♥A and the remaining ♠J doubleton will represent a certain 4th trick for the defense.

South's only chance is if one of the defenders now has a singleton ♠J. South should continue with the ♠Q in the hope that the ♠J will be pinned under it. The defense will win the ♠K and the best they can do is to take the ♥A in order to stop South from making an overtrick by later discarding both of his remaining hearts on dummy's diamonds. South can later draw the rest of the trump and make his contract.

notes: West leads the ♣K against 4♥. West wins the first 2 tricks in clubs and switches to a trump. The straightforward play is to draw a second round of trump and to pass the ♦J for a finesse. On the actual layout, East wins the ♦K, and when the spade finesse loses, the contract fails.

South was unlucky to lose both finesses, but given West's initial pass it was possible for South to guarantee the contract. West had shown up with the ♣A and ♣K so he could not have both of the missing Kings as well. With both the ♠K and the ♦K, West would have had at least 13 high card points and he would have opened the bidding.

South should win the second round of trump in the dummy and continue with a low diamond toward the ♦J. If East has the ♦K, he must win the trick (or else South will have avoided a diamond loser and will not mind if the spade finesse loses). If East returns a spade, South can win the ♠A, unblock the ♦J, and cross to the dummy in hearts. Dummy's 2 diamond winners can then be used to discard South's 2 spade losers.

If West was dealt the ♦K, he will take South's ♦J. However, South can now be certain that East was dealt the ♠K and he can finesse in that suit in order to make the contract. If West was dealt the ♠K in addition to the ♣A, ♣K, and ♦K that he has already played, he certainly would have opened the bidding.

West's opening bid marks him with most of the outstanding high cards (certainly the ♠A and ♣AQ). South will have to lose at least those two Aces and a trump trick so he should play to minimize his chances of having to lose a 2nd club trick as well.

South should lead a trump from dummy at trick 2. If East follows with the ♠4, South should follow with a low spade from his hand, allowing West to win the trick cheaply. West can do no better than return a heart to the dummy. South can continue trump, playing an honor from his hand to force West's ♠A. West might as well cash the ♣A at this point to prevent an overtrick (as South is now in a position to draw East's last trump and run the diamonds).

If East plays the ♠9, ♠10, or ♠J on the first round of trump, South must cover with the ♠K or ♠Q to force West's ♠A. West returns a heart to the dummy and East follows with the ♠4 on the second round of trump. South should play a low spade on this trick to make sure that West wins the second trump trick for the defense. As before, West must cash the ♣A to prevent an overtrick. Otherwise, South would be able to draw East's last trump and run diamonds to discard his clubs.

notes: West leads the ♠10 against 6NT. There are 10 top tricks (3 spades, 3 hearts, 1 diamond, and 3 clubs). The diamond finesse could provide South with an extra trick and it should be possible for South to develop at least one extra trick in clubs.

After winning West's spade opening lead, South should finesse East for the ♦K before he touches the club suit. When the diamond finesse wins, South's total is up to 11 tricks. As only 1 extra club trick is now required, South should start the suit by leading toward dummy's ♣10. This is a safety play against West having 5 clubs headed by the ♣J.

On the actual layout, West will win the ♣J. South can win any return that West makes, unblock the ♣10, and easily win the rest of the tricks. If the diamond finesse had lost to the ♦K with West, South would need 2 extra tricks from clubs and he would know to play that suit from the top, hoping for a 3-3 break.

The correct play in clubs depends on whether South needs 4 or 5 tricks from that suit. Taking the diamond finesse first is a discovery play that will let South know how many clubs tricks are required (and how that suit should be played).

notes: West leads the ♠Q against 2♥. South must lose a trick to the ♥A, but with only 4 side suit losers (1 in spades, 2 in diamonds, and 1 in clubs) the contract looks secure. West's 1♠ overcall warns South that the defense may be in a position to defeat the contract by winning a trick with a spade ruff.

If South makes the mistake of winning the first trick with the ♠K, the contract will fail. South continues by driving out West's ♥A, but West will continue spades and East will ruff dummy's ♠A (it would not help declarer to duck this trick in dummy). South will be left with 4 inescapable losers (1 spade, 2 diamonds, and 1 club).

This danger can be avoided by winning dummy's ♠A at trick 1. A heart is played to drive out West's ♥A and West will play a second round of spades. If East ruffs this trick he will be ruffing South's spade loser. There is no quick entry to the West hand for East to get another spade ruff, and the contract will be secure. South can win any return and draw trump to lose only 3 minor suit tricks at the end.

If instead East chooses to discard on the second round of spades, the result will be the same. South will win the ♠K and draw the rest of the trump. South will still have to lose the spade trick he was budgeting for (along with 2 diamond tricks and a club trick), but the contract will be made.

notes: West leads the ♥K against 4♠. West's ♥K wins the first trick and his club shift presents South with a guess a trick 2. If South misguesses and plays the wrong club from dummy, then 2 club tricks will have to be lost. If there is also a trump loser then the contract will fail.

As there are 8 spades between the North-South hands, declarer should plan to finesse East for the ♠Q. If East has that card then it won't matter if South misguesses in clubs. South should, therefore, think about the worst case and assume that West has the ♠Q and that a trump trick will have to be lost. Using this reasoning (called 'second-degree assumption' by Reese) South can deduce the correct play in clubs.

West's lead of the ♥K strongly suggests that he was dealt the ♥A as well. Under the assumption that West has the ♠Q (otherwise the contract will be easy), West cannot have the ♣A. That would give West 13 HCP, but West passed in first seat. It is possible that West has the ♣Q so South should play the ♣10 or ♣J from the dummy.

On the actual layout, South's club play is irrelevant as East, who was dealt both the ♣A and ♣Q, wins the next 2 tricks in that suit. When East returns a heart, South should be careful to ruff with a middle trump, preserving the ♠7.

South must now avoid losing a trump trick and will have to hope that the ♠Q is with East, but it would be wrong to lay down a top honor before crossing to dummy for a finesse. To do so would gain if West were dealt a singleton ♠Q, but if West has a singleton spade it is 4 times as likely to be a low card. Laying down a high trump would be fatal on the above layout of the East-West cards.

Instead, South should cross to the dummy in diamonds and take a first round spade finesse by passing dummy's ♠8. Thanks to South's thoughtful ruff with a middle trump on the second round of hearts, the lead is still in the dummy and the trump finesse can be repeated. By playing in this manner South has to cross to the dummy only once in diamonds, minimizing the risk of a defensive ruff in that suit.

notes: West leads the ♥K against 4♠. West wins the first trick and continues with the ♥A which wins as East completes an echo. West continues with a third round of hearts which increases the danger that a trump trick could be lost. The bidding and East's heart signals strongly suggest that East is out of hearts.

If South ruffs with dummy's ♠10 or ♠9 there is a danger that East will overuff with the ♠J and return a trump. The 4-2 club break means that South lacks the dummy entries required to establish and cash a winner in that suit. In the fullness of time South will lose a diamond trick and the contract will be defeated.

On the above layout, South can succeed by ruffing the third round of hearts with dummy's ♠K and finessing East for the ♠J. If West was dealt the ♠J, however, he will win the trick. As before, South will have no way to avoid a diamond loser at the end.

South's best chance is to discard a diamond loser from the dummy at trick 3 (a so-called loser-on-loser play). East can do no better than ruff and return a diamond to South. South will later be able to ruff his diamond loser in the dummy and win the rest of the tricks to make his contract.

If West was dealt 3 spades headed by the ♠J and a doubleton diamond, it is critical that the ♠K is still in dummy when South tries to ruff his diamond loser (otherwise West would be able to ruff with the ♠J in front of the dummy to take the setting trick). On this layout South can afford to draw at most 1 round of trump (with either the ♠A or ♠Q) before he ruffs his diamond loser.

notes: West leads the ♠J against 4NT. South has 8 top tricks (4 diamonds and 4 clubs). South can come to an extra trick in both spades and hearts, but careful play is required in order to avoid losing several tricks in one of the major suits.

When East follows small to the first trick, South has a critical decision to make. If South wins the ♠Q or ♠K the contract will fail. East will eventually gain the lead with the ♥A and a spade return by East through South's remaining honor will allow the defense to run that suit.

West's weak 2♠ opening suggests that the actual layout of the majors is to be expected. South can neutralize West's spade suit by playing the ♠2 from his hand at trick 1! The result of this hold up play is that, if West continues spades to clear the suit, East will be unable to return a spade after winning his ♥A.

West does better by switching to the ♥10 after the ♠J holds the first trick (instead of clearing the spades). Once again South must be alert - if he plays a low heart from the dummy the contract will fail. East will play low and South's ♥K will win the trick (ducking the ♥K would be immediately fatal as the defenders are in a position to cash their major-suit Aces to set the contract).

South will have to knock out the ♠A in order to come to 10 tricks, but the defense will now be in a position to run the heart suit and defeat 4NT. South can counter this danger by covering West's ♥10 switch with dummy's ♥Q (second hand high). East must win the ♥A in order to cause any problem, but he cannot afford to continue hearts without giving South a trick with dummy's ♥9.
In practice, East will revert to spades, but in doing so he will be helping to set up South's 10th trick (not that it matters - the contract is now safe regardless of what East returns).

South has lost only 3 tricks. He has established the 2 extra winners he needs and now has full control of both major suits. South can win whatever suit West returns and easily win the balance of the tricks to make the contract.

notes: West leads the ♥10 against 6♦ doubled. East's double of 6♦ was a Lightner double, requesting the opening lead of dummy's first bid suit. South is able to ruff West's heart opening lead. The ♣A must be lost and South must play with care in order to avoid promoting a trump trick for West.

South should plan to ruff both of his spade losers in the dummy. Proper timing involves immediately cashing the ♠A and ♠K and then ruffing a spade in the dummy. It would be a mistake to return to the South hand with a heart ruff in order to ruff the last spade loser in the dummy. After cashing the ♦A, South would have no way to prevent West from scoring a trump trick.

Ruffing another heart in hand would promote West's trump holding into the setting trick immediately. If instead South leads a club at this point, East will win the ♣A in order to play a heart himself, similarly promoting the setting trick in trump.

South can prevent this danger by leading a club after ruffing a spade in dummy (instead of ruffing a heart in the South hand). East can do no better than win the ♣A and return a high heart for South to ruff low. South continues by ruffing his last spade in the dummy and cashing the ♦A. Thanks to South's careful play, he can return to his hand safely in clubs to draw the rest of the trump and win the balance of the tricks.

Another trap on this deal is to play on clubs at trick 2. After winning the ♣A, East would return a high heart for South to ruff. The best South can do is cash his top spades and ruff a spade in dummy. South can return to his hand in clubs to ruff his last spade in dummy, but after cashing the ♦A, the dummy will be down to just hearts and West's diamonds will be promoted as before.

South can (and should) guard against this danger by refusing to cover East's ♠J at trick 2. This unusual refusal to cover allows South to retain his spade stopper while exhausting East (the dangerous opponent) of spades. East will continue spades to West's ♠K (no other suit is better) and West is welcome to clear the suit.

South must play on diamonds to come close to 9 tricks. He can afford to lose a diamond trick as long as East does not gain the lead.

South should lead a low diamond from the dummy at trick 2. When East follows small, South should play the ♦9 from his hand. West is welcome to win this trick, but he cannot attack hearts profitably from his side of the table. South should win West's club return with dummy's ♣A and unblock the diamonds. South can now cross to the ♠K in order to cash dummy's 3 remaining diamond winners. The ♠A will be South's 9th trick.

If South had to play diamonds for 6 tricks, the percentage play would be to cash the ♦A and ♦K hoping for the ♦Q to drop. On this deal it would be wrong to play this way as East would win the ♦Q on the third round and lead a heart through South's ♥K to defeat 3NT. Given that South can afford to lose a diamond trick, he should take the recommended line in order to minimize the chances of having to lose that trick to East.

notes: West leads the ♠Q against 3NT. The blockage in the club suit and the fact that dummy has no sure entry makes this problem more difficult than it first appears. South can, in fact, guarantee the contract, but only by playing the first several tricks in a specific order.

South must win West's spade opening lead and immediately unblock the club suit by cashing the ♣A, ♣K, and ♣Q. South must continue with the ♦K from hand. This places the defenders in a no-win situation. If West takes the ♦A, the ♦Q will become an entry to the long club suit in dummy. With 2 spade tricks, the ♦Q, and 6 club tricks, South will make his contract without a single trick from the heart suit.

If instead West chooses to duck his ♦A, South will have a diamond trick in the bag. South can now turn his attention to hearts and lead that suit to force out the ♥A. West can do no better than return a spade to South, but South has won 6 tricks at this point and his 3 heart winners will be enough to secure the contract.

On the assumption that the defenders' spades were dealt 4-4, South can afford to lose a club trick (as he will lose only 4 tricks in total - 1 club and 3 spades). South should duck the first round of clubs completely as a safety play against West holding all 4 outstanding clubs.

East's discard on the first round of clubs reveals the 4-0 club break so that South's first-round club duck was a necessary precaution. The defense will cash a spade trick and play a heart to South. South easily wins the rest of the tricks with the help of the marked finesse in clubs. If both defenders had followed to the first round of clubs, the suit would now run as cashing the ♣A and ♣K would drop all the remaining clubs.

West wins the second round of diamonds and forces South's last trump with his club return. South is out of trump and out of tricks. West will win the third round of diamonds, leaving the defense in a position to win the rest of the tricks.

South can avoid this danger by starting on diamonds at trick 2. East wins the first round and forces South to ruff a heart. South continues with 4 rounds of trump followed by a second round of diamonds to West. South can ruff the return and drive out West's last diamond honor. South still has a trump left and he can win West's return and take the last 2 tricks in diamonds.

The recommended line of play only loses when the East-West spades are 3-3 and West was dealt the ♦AKQx(x), or if East holds those diamonds which is rather unlikely in view of his pre-emptive 4♥ opening. West would certainly select a diamond as his opening lead with the ♦AKQ so, as a practical matter, the recommended line can only gain. Furthermore, the recommended line is necessary given the actual 4-2 spade break.

notes: West leads the ♣Q against 4♥. After South wins West's club opening lead, it seems intuitive to drive out the ♥A immediately. The problem with this plan is that the defense will continue clubs to knock out South's other high honor. The fate of the contract will now depend on the position of the ♦K.

South can double his chances for success by finessing in diamonds before playing trump (leading to dummy's ♦Q is best, but leading to dummy's ♦10 is also acceptable). If the diamond finesse had won, South would turn his attention to the trump suit, but when East wins the ♦K and clears clubs, South's only chance is to finesse West for the ♦J immediately.

When the second diamond finesse wins, the ♦A is cashed for a club discard. It is now safe to drive out the ♥A. South can ruff the club return, draw trump, and establish a trick in spades. The South hand is now high and the contract will be made.

Any reasonable line of play will succeed when West was dealt the ♦K. The recommended line is best because it also results in success on most layouts in which East was dealt the ♦K and West was dealt the ♦J.

notes: West leads the ♥J against 4♠. West's heart opening lead is taken by South with the ♥A. East's 1NT opening marks him with most of the outstanding high cards so it looks like South should be able to hold his losers to 1 spade and 2 clubs.

The main danger to the contract is that East might have all 4 outstanding spades. In this case, South can prevent East from winning 2 trump tricks by starting the suit with a low card to dummy's ♠J. West's discard confirms the 4-0 trump break and East takes dummy's ♠J with the ♠A. East returns a heart.

It would be a mistake for South to ruff this trick. The best South could then do is cross to the dummy in diamonds in order to lead a second round of trump toward the closed hand. East would insert the ♠8 to force an honor from South. South would continue with another diamond to the dummy to finesse again in trump.

South is now in trouble. If he draws East's last trump and crosses to the dummy in diamonds in order to play a club toward his ♣K, East will take the ♣A and cash heart tricks to defeat the contract. If South tries to set up a club trick while a trump remains outstanding (so that the dummy's last trump can be used to ruff the next round of hearts) the contract will fail on the actual layout as East will be able to ruff the third round of diamonds.

South can maintain trump control by discarding a club loser on the second round of hearts. If East continues hearts South can take the ruff in the dummy and maintain trump control. If instead East defends passively by returning a diamond, South wins in the dummy in order to play a trump through East. South can return to the dummy in diamonds, finesse against East's ♠10, and draw the last trump.

Now that East is out of trump it is safe to cross to the dummy a third time in diamonds. South continues with a club toward the ♣K which East takes with the ♣A. South has a trump remaining to handle a force from East. South will win the last 2 tricks with his remaining diamond and the ♣K and make the contract.
